# Toast at Four

I finished my last night shift at half past seven on Sunday morning. Saturday 7th November, nine at night until half seven, majors, like all the others. Fourteen years of nights and the last one was unremarkable, which is what I'd asked for and also, somehow, not what I wanted at all.

I drove home down the London Road with the sun coming up in front of me and the shipping forecast on catch-up, because that's one of the small indignities of nights: you never hear it live, so it arrives a day late, like a letter. Somewhere along the London Road I worked out that I wouldn't see that light from this side again. It's the same sun from the day rota. It just comes at you from the other direction.

My first night was in 2012, as an SHO. I remember very little of it except the car park afterwards, sitting in the dark at the Infirmary, crying, because I couldn't remember whether I'd given the second dose. I had. I sat there long enough for the windscreen to frost over, and I can still picture that frost, which is strange, because I genuinely cannot tell you what I had for lunch on Tuesday.

## What people think nights are

People assume nights are about adrenaline. Some of it is. There are hours that go very fast and that I won't write about here.

But most of a night isn't adrenaline. Most of it is endurance, and the thing you are actually trying to do at five in the morning, when you are empty and your feet hurt and the vending machine has eaten your last coin, is stay kind. That's the job. Not the procedures, not the decisions — those matter, obviously, but they're the easy part compared to being a decent human being at five a.m. when you've got nothing left in the tank.

Nights are where the department is most itself. Fewer managers. Fewer meetings. Nobody performing for anyone. The people who are there are there because they have to be, and that makes for a kind of honesty you don't get at eleven in the morning. There's less politeness and more kindness. Those aren't the same thing and on nights you learn the difference.

I had an old gentleman in last winter, around three in the morning, who took my hand and told me I had his daughter's hands. He went home three days later. I'm not going to say any more about him than that. But I've thought about it a lot since, and I don't think I was doing anything particularly clever at the time.

And then there's the toast.

## The toast

At four o'clock, someone makes toast in the staff room. Nobody admits to starting it. It simply appears, every night, and there's always too much of it, and it's always slightly burnt on one side because the toaster has been on its last legs since roughly 2019. There's a rota for most things in that department but there has never been a rota for the toast. It just happens.

I have eaten toast at four in the morning with people I would not otherwise have met, from countries I've never been to, who I would now trust with anything. I have eaten it in silence with someone who'd just had a terrible hour and didn't want to talk. I have eaten it with Folasade, who has done nights for twenty-two years and still beats me up the stairs. Twenty-two years. She doesn't mention it. She just goes up the stairs faster than I do and waits at the top with a face like she's got all day.

Fourteen years is nothing next to that. It's also long enough.

## What it took

I'm not going to write about staffing. I've written those pieces, I stand by them, and nothing in this one is a complaint about the rota or the numbers.

This is the other thing, the smaller thing that nobody puts in a report.

I missed both my nieces' naming ceremonies. Both of them, on video, from a laptop on a desk in a room with no windows. My sister was in Bangalore for both and she never once complained. Not a word, not a sigh, nothing I could hang a guilt on. I'd have preferred it if she had. She'll read this and say something dry about how I've finally got a proper job. She'll be right.

And the body keeps its own accounts. My knees have opinions now. My sleep has been a rumour for years. In September my GP used the phrase "not a joke anymore" about my blood pressure, and I've been an emergency physician for long enough to know that when a GP says that about you, you listen.

So: days only, from Monday. Which is the right thing. Which is also, and I want to be honest about this, a loss.

## The traitor bit

I'm relieved, and I feel like a traitor for being relieved.

Both of those are true. Neither cancels the other out. I have spent fourteen years telling anyone who'd listen that nights are the best part of the job, and I still think that, and I'm still leaving them, and I still want to go. I don't know how to hold all that at once, so I'm writing it down instead.

I'll miss being in the building when it's quiet enough to hear what it actually sounds like. I'll miss the particular comradeship of people who are all awake at a time when they shouldn't be. I'll miss the version of myself who could do it — who could stay kind at five a.m., most nights, and pick himself up and go again the next one.

I won't miss the drive home with the sun in my eyes and my hands shaking slightly on the wheel. I won't miss the frost.

## The last bit

Folasade is still on nights. She'll be on them long after I've gone, and she'll still be faster up the stairs than whoever replaces me, and she will not want a fuss made about any of this. So I won't make one.

But somewhere at four o'clock tomorrow morning, someone in that staff room will make toast. It won't be anybody's job. Nobody will have asked for it. It'll just appear, slightly burnt on one side, and a handful of tired people will eat it and feel a bit more human, and then they'll go back out and get on with it.

That's the part I'm sorry to leave. Not the drama — there's plenty of that on days. The toast.

Go careful up the stairs, Folasade. I'll see you on the other side of the rota.
